ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c0.text
Art of Asia: In China, beautiful handwriting was long considered the highest of the arts, above painting. A single brushstroke was thought to reveal the writer's character.\n\nCalligraphers used the "four treasures of the study": brush, ink stick, ink stone and paper. Ink cannot be erased, so every stroke has to be right the first time.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c1.text
Art of Asia: Chinese painters called landscape shanshui, "mountains and water". From the Song dynasty onward it became the most prestigious subject of painting.\n\nPainters used black ink in many shades, and left empty space for mist, water and sky. Scrolls were meant to be read slowly, like a journey through the hills.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c2.text
Art of Asia: Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world": the pleasure districts, theatres and fashions of Edo, today's Tokyo, from the 1600s to the 1800s.\n\nMost were colour woodblock prints, sold cheaply to ordinary townspeople. Their stars included Utamaro, Hokusai and Hiroshige, whose views of Mount Fuji and the Tōkaidō road became best-sellers.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c3.text
Art of Asia: When Japan opened to Western trade in the 1850s, its prints flooded into Europe. Hokusai's *Great Wave* and Hiroshige's views struck Paris artists as something completely new.\n\nMonet, Degas, Van Gogh and Mary Cassatt borrowed flat colour, bold outlines, off-centre views and everyday subjects. The craze was called japonisme.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c4.text
Art of Asia: Hindu temples in India were designed as homes for the gods and models of the cosmos, their towers rising like the sacred mountain at the centre of the world.\n\nTheir walls are covered with sculpture: gods, dancers, animals, lovers and scenes from epic stories. At Ellora, a whole temple was carved downwards out of a single cliff.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c5.text
Art of Asia: The Mughal emperors, who ruled much of South Asia from 1526, ran royal workshops that produced exquisite small paintings for books and albums.\n\nPersian and Indian artists worked side by side, and later borrowed ideas from European prints. The results include court histories, portraits and astonishingly precise studies of birds, animals and flowers.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c6.text
Art of Asia: Mosques and many religious buildings avoid pictures of people and animals. Instead, artists developed dazzling ornament from geometry, flowing plant forms and calligraphy.\n\nWith only a compass and a ruler, they built complex star patterns that repeat endlessly across tiles, wood, plaster and metal, from Spain to Central Asia.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c7.text
Art of Asia: Angkor Wat, in Cambodia, was built in the early 1100s by the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later became Buddhist and is still used today.\n\nIt is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its wide moat for the ocean around it.

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c8.text
Art of Asia: Porcelain is a fine white ceramic made from kaolin clay fired at about 1,300 °C. It is hard, thin and translucent, and for centuries only China knew how to make it.\n\nChinese porcelain was traded across Asia and Africa and, from the 1500s, shipped to Europe in huge quantities. In English it simply became "china".

ar-asia.title: ar-asia.c9.text
Art of Asia: During the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), Korean potters made celadon: stoneware with a soft blue-green glaze admired across East Asia for its jade-like colour.\n\nThey also invented an inlay technique, sanggam: designs were carved into the clay and filled with white and black slip before glazing, giving delicate cranes, clouds and willows.
